name: Fullerene (C60)

card.summary: A hollow 60-carbon molecule, also called buckminsterfullerene, used in some skincare as a free-radical-scavenging antioxidant aimed at wrinkles and acne.
card.note: Cosmetic fullerene studies are small and mostly early; toxicity depends on the form and route.

quick.overview:
Fullerene C60 is a cage-shaped carbon molecule with 60 atoms arranged like a football. In skincare it is sold as an antioxidant, often dissolved in oils such as squalane, with the aim of reducing wrinkles and breakouts and improving skin quality.

Research includes small human trials of C60 in squalane for wrinkles, a clinical trial of topical fullerene for acne, a trial of a fullerene water complex on collagen quality and a 2026 phase II trial in radiation dermatitis. A review describes fullerenes as scavengers of reactive oxygen species with anti-ageing potential.
quick.how: In cosmetics, C60 appears in creams and serums where it is dissolved in an oil or carrier. Users apply it topically as part of a routine. Some people also take C60 in oil by mouth for wellness, which is a separate and less studied use.
quick.risks: Toxicity depends on dose, exposure time, the type of fullerene, functional groups and route; a 2013 review cited on Wikipedia found very little evidence that C60 is toxic. Animal studies have examined inhalation and intravenous exposure. Cosmetic products are not regulated as drugs.

lead: Fullerene C60, or buckminsterfullerene, is a carbon molecule with 60 atoms arranged as a truncated icosahedron, like a football [1]. It was discovered in 1985 by Harold Kroto, James Heath, Sean O'Brien, Robert Curl and Richard Smalley, and Kroto, Curl and Smalley received the 1996 Nobel Prize in Chemistry [1].

In appearance terms, C60 is used in skincare as an antioxidant. A review of fullerenes as anti-ageing antioxidants discusses their ability to scavenge reactive oxygen species and act as mild mitochondrial uncouplers [2]. Human studies have looked at C60 dissolved in squalane for anti-wrinkle effects [3], topical fullerene for acne [4] and a fullerene water complex for collagen quality and skin function [5].
A 2026 phase II double-blind trial compared fullerene with trolamine for acute radiation dermatitis in head and neck cancer patients [6].

chain: Oxidative stress on skin is reduced
angle.text: C60 products are applied to the skin as antioxidants, with trials examining wrinkles, acne and collagen quality. The proposed route to looks is through reduced oxidative damage.

paras: Cosmetic uses center on topical antioxidant products. The anti-ageing literature discusses fullerenes' radical-scavenging capacity [2]. Fullerene-based systems have also been proposed for drug delivery [7], and biomedical applications named in encyclopedias include MRI contrast agents and photodynamic tumour therapy [1].

A 2017 review proposes that fullerenes can act as mitochondrial protonophores and scavenge reactive oxygen species, based on simulations of transport through lipid membranes together with experimental data, and also covers toxicity and therapeutic use [2].

A 2013 review cited by Wikipedia found very little evidence from studies since the discovery of fullerenes that C60 is toxic, with toxicity depending on dose, exposure time, fullerene type, functional groups used for water solubility and route of administration [1]. Animal studies have examined disposition after intratracheal or intravenous administration [8] and effects on the lung from inhalation or instillation [9].

Human studies of fullerene in skin include a randomized clinical evaluation of C60 dissolved in squalane for anti-wrinkle cosmetics (2010) [3], a clinical trial of topical fullerene for acne vulgaris (2011) [4], a randomized trial of a hyper-harmonized fullerene water complex on collagen quality and skin function (2020) [5], and a 2026 phase II double-blind randomized trial of fullerene versus trolamine for acute radiation dermatitis in head and neck cancer [6]. The titles of these studies are listed here; readers should consult the papers for outcomes.
